content: The benefits of palliative care are most pronounced when it is introduced early in the course of an illness. In some cases, early palliative care has been linked to prolonged survival. However, there is less data available on the outcomes of palliative care for children compared to adults. Pediatric palliative care (PPC) has been associated with improvements in health-related quality of life, emotional well-being, and family satisfaction. Evidence suggests that integrating palliative care into healthcare systems enhances their ability to fulfill their mission of improving the well-being of those they serve. Palliative care should not be viewed solely as an alternative to curative or life-sustaining treatments of uncertain benefit. Instead, it should be considered an essential complement to curative or disease-modifying treatments for serious or life-threatening health conditions. Adherence to curative or disease-modifying treatments can be challenging when disease symptoms or treatment side effects are not adequately managed. Palliative care can improve adherence, particularly to toxic treatments such as those for drug-resistant tuberculosis and many cancers. Among impoverished populations, poverty and social challenges often exacerbate difficulties in adhering to treatment. In lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), treatment abandonment—failure to initiate or complete medically indicated curative therapy—is a major cause of therapeutic failure in potentially curable childhood cancers. Financial difficulties, distress from side effects, and poor relationships with healthcare workers are common reasons for treatment abandonment. PPC has the potential to address these issues. Social supports, as described in other contexts, have also been shown to reduce treatment abandonment and improve adherence. Palliative care not only enhances patient comfort but also strengthens healthcare systems' ability to effectively treat serious and life-threatening conditions. In many countries, patients and their families bear the majority of the burden of caring for individuals with serious health problems. Families of medically ill children often face profound social and economic challenges, including isolation, loss of income, and catastrophic healthcare expenses. Family caregivers, often women or children, may be unable to work, attend school, or participate in social activities due to caregiving demands. In low-income settings, family caregivers frequently must leave income-generating activities or other responsibilities to accompany patients to hospitals, putting families at risk of financial ruin and caregivers at risk of exhaustion and health problems. Integrating palliative care into pediatric healthcare can reduce costs for both families and healthcare systems. Studies from high-income countries (HICs) indicate that palliative care can lower expenses for patients, families, and health systems. Community-based and home care networks allow patients to remain at home and comfortable, reducing the need for hospital visits for symptom relief. These networks can also decrease the demand for expensive, non-beneficial disease-modifying treatments near the end of life by offering compassionate alternatives and supportive counseling. Additionally, they can shorten hospital stays by making symptom control accessible in the community. Families are spared the costs of unnecessary hospital admissions, including transportation, co-payments, and lodging expenses. Family caregivers may be able to continue working part-time, and child caregivers may remain in school. Palliative care integration also reduces healthcare system costs by decreasing unnecessary resource utilization. As populations age and the prevalence of chronic non-communicable diseases rises, a growing portion of healthcare budgets is spent on aggressive, often non-beneficial treatments near the end of life. Palliative care, integrated at all levels of healthcare systems, can reduce these costs while improving outcomes. Home-based palliative care offers additional benefits for public health. Community health workers (CHWs), nurses, and mobile palliative care teams visiting patients at home can provide primary prevention and screening interventions, such as education on smoking cessation, indoor air quality, diet, exercise, prenatal care, vaccinations, and cancer screening. Strengthening home care capacity for palliative care also enhances disease prevention and early diagnosis. Communication links established for palliative care can reduce loss to follow-up, ensuring patients keep appointments and receive necessary care. Palliative care is essential for achieving universal health coverage (UHC) and Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3, which aims to ensure access to quality health services without financial hardship. The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes palliative care as part of UHC, encompassing the full spectrum of essential health services, including health promotion, prevention, treatment, rehabilitation, and palliative care. However, there is a significant lack of evidence on pediatric palliative care, particularly in LMICs, where the majority of patients in need reside. Barriers to palliative care research include difficulty identifying measurable outcomes, lack of funding, absence of research strategies, inadequate infrastructure, and overwhelming patient loads in LMICs. Research priorities for pediatric palliative care include assessing the needs of children in specific locations, evaluating interventions for pain and symptom management, studying clinical outcomes such as quality of life, and determining the effectiveness of training programs. Additional areas of focus include understanding cultural and religious attitudes toward illness and death, addressing healthcare provider attitudes, and investigating the cost-effectiveness of palliative care. Research is also needed to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of palliative treatments in children, including alternative opioids, neuropathic pain management, and opioid rotation protocols. WHO has proposed detailed priorities for research on managing persistent pain in children, emphasizing the need for evidence-based approaches to improve care. Ongoing data collection on the integration, accessibility, quality, and outcomes of pediatric palliative care is crucial. This includes assessing the degree of integration into healthcare systems and identifying gaps in service delivery. Data collection tools, such as the Palliative Outcomes Scale, can provide valuable insights for both researchers and clinicians. These tools should be concise, address all types of suffering, and be adaptable for routine use in clinical settings. Understanding the cultural, religious, and personal experiences of children and families is essential for designing effective palliative care services. Research on healthcare provider attitudes, including addressing irrational fears of prescribing opioids, can improve care and outcomes.
